# Showing things to the person

You can drive their view, not just the design. When they ask to see something, show it: do not tell them where to click.

```
./ise view select L26          select it, open its properties, frame it
./ise view isolate L26         show only it (and frame it)
./ise view frame L30–L32       frame it, keep everything visible
./ise view show_all            everything visible again, framed
./ise view hide L19 / show L19 hide or show one item
./ise view color status        paint the building by sale status (color material to undo)
./ise view camera top          iso, front, back, left, right, top, bottom (glides there, everything framed)
./ise view explode Bracket 1.5 pull an assembly's parts apart (spread 0.25–2.5, default 1); `off` puts them back
./ise view camera 35,20,20,0.85   any direction: azimuth (0 from the front, 90 from the right), elevation, and optionally the lens's vertical angle (default 36°; 15–25° for product shots with little perspective) and how much of the frame what is shown fills (0.85: a product shot framed tight and centred; left out: framed loosely); straight down (elevation 90) the azimuth says which way is up, as if the camera had tilted up from there (90,90: the +X end at the bottom)
./ise view render              photoreal render mode: the view path-traced live (studio light, physical metals, plastics, glass); `render white` in the white sweep
./ise view projection ortho    orthographic (true elevations) or perspective
./ise view display edges       shaded, edges, wireframe, hidden (hidden line) or xray; zebra, curvature or draft (surface analysis)
./ise view section x 25        cut at x = 25 mm, cut faces filled and hatched (add `flip` to keep the other side; one plane per axis, together a section box)
./ise view section box x0 y0 z0 x1 y1 z1   six planes round a region (bare `box`: the model's middle); `section off` clears
./ise view measure Block Pin    measure one item (mass, inertia) or one to another in their view, with dimension lines
```

For a website's 3D viewer, `./ise render --glb product.glb` writes what the view shows as a binary glTF with the same materials and printed labels as the renders (metres, Y up, centred, on the ground; isolate the product first), ready for `<model-viewer>`, Shopify or WooCommerce 3D and AR on phones; the person has the same as Save 3D for web in render mode. `./ise render [--width 1920] [--height 1080] [--samples 256] [--studio white] [--out shot.png]` writes a photoreal PNG of the model as their view shows it (set the camera, isolation and explode first; a square or upright image keeps everything the view shows across); with no view open it renders in a headless browser. `--studio white` is a product shot: a seamless white sweep (floor and backdrop one pure white, the model's soft shadows on it, true colours), as catalogue and listing photos are; the default is the grey studio. For a product shot, isolate the item, choose the view (`view camera 30,22,20,0.85`: a narrow lens keeps it from looking distorted, 0.85 frames it tight), render at 1024 samples or more for a clean image, and look at the result. Materials render from their names: metals by family (aluminium, steel, stainless, brass, copper), a colour word or a hex in the name colours it ("Aluminium 5052 anodised black" renders anodised, "PC/ABS yellow #f9cf00" that exact yellow), plastics by theirs (ABS, PC, POM, TPE, rubber, epoxy dome labels), finish words set the surface (polished, satin, brushed, bead blasted, matte, gloss, chrome for a mirror plate, clear for see-through; translucent lets light through, a coloured one glowing its colour), glass, acrylic and LED epoxy transmit light (clear ones letting light through to what is under them). Surface textures from the name too: stippled or pebbled for a rubber grip's pebbles; textured (or grained, mould texture) on a plastic for the fine grain a mould gives a matte housing (write "ABS (yellow #f2b805, matte textured)" for a moulded body, not satin, which reads as smooth painted plastic); brushed or hairline on a metal for the abrasive's fine lines. A badge or domed label is its pieces: a gloss epoxy dome over the print, chrome foil for metallic lettering and rims. The white sweep lights as a product photographer does, turned to the camera for every shot: black cards round the camera, a big softbox on its left, the white sweep behind, so gloss, chrome and steel read as themselves. Printed labels and logos go on as printed pictures (see Pictures); etched and moulded markings are modelled. Photo skins: `./ise render --skin "Left side,Right side,Top"` (also with `--glb`) lays those calibrated canvases back onto the model, each onto the faces that look toward its camera and that it saw, so every line, groove, logo, button and print of the real product shows exactly as photographed (plastics, rubber and print take it; metals and see-through parts keep their own finish; faces no photo saw keep the modelled material). The skin is kept for the renders that follow; `--skin none` clears it. With a skin every modelled raised or sunk detail must sit exactly where the photos show it, or not be modelled: anything invented or misplaced shows twice. Renders show the design, not the view's selection, x-ray or picked-piece tints.

Names work (instances like L26, shapes, assemblies) or ids. These change only that person's view (the person who spoke to you last, also after the engine restarts; before anyone has spoken, every open view of the project); nothing is saved and other people's views stay as they are. The context tells you what their view shows (selection, isolation, hidden items, paint).
